{{Short description|Specialized typewriter or chorded keyboard for recording in shorthand}}
{{Globalize|article|USA|2name=the United States|date=December 2010}}
[[File:Demonstratie met een stenotypemachine Weeknummer 28-28 - Open Beelden - 22262.ogv|thumb|Demonstration Marc Grandjean (1928)]]
A '''steno machine''', '''stenotype machine''', '''shorthand machine''', '''stenograph''' or '''steno writer''' is a specialized [[chorded keyboard]] or [[typewriter]] used by [[stenographers]] for [[shorthand]] use. In order to pass the United States [[Registered Professional Reporter]] test, a trained [[court reporter]] or [[Closed captioning|closed captioner]] must write speeds of approximately 180, 200, and 225 [[words per minute]] (wpm) at very high accuracy in the categories of literary, jury charge, and testimony, respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.captions.org/2006/02/captioning-students-thoughts.html |title=Closed Captioning Web |publisher=Captions.org |date=2006-02-13 |access-date=2013-01-14 |url-status=unfit |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060310062955/http://www.captions.org/2006/02/captioning-students-thoughts.html |archive-date=March 10, 2006 }}</ref> Some stenographers can reach up to 375 words per minute, according to the website of the [[California]] Official Court Reporters Association (COCRA).<ref>{{cite web|title=COCRA – Read/Write Like a Court Reporter – California Official Court Reporters Association|url=https://cocra.org/?s=375 |work=California Official Court Reporters Association|date=July 6, 2012 | access-date=August 1, 2019}}</ref>

The stenotype keyboard has far fewer keys than a conventional [[alphanumeric keyboard]]. Multiple keys are pressed simultaneously (known as "[[chorded keyboard|chording]]" or "stroking") to spell out whole [[syllable]]s, words, and phrases with a single hand motion. This system makes [[real-time transcription|realtime transcription]] practical for [[court reporting]] and live [[closed captioning]]. Because the keyboard does not contain all the letters of the English alphabet, letter combinations are substituted for the missing letters. There are several schools of thought on how to record various sounds, such as the StenEd, Phoenix, and Magnum Steno theories.

==History==
[[File:Stenograph 1a, Miles Bartholomew.jpg|thumb|Stenograph - first model, Miles Bartholomew, 1879]]
The first shorthand machine (the word "stenotype" was not used for another 80 years or more) punched a paper strip and was built in 1830 by [[Karl Drais]], a German inventor.<ref>Karl Drais-The New Biography by Dr. Hans-Erhard Lessing</ref> The first machine was made in 1863 by the Italian [[Antonio Michela Zucco]] and was in actual use from 1880 in the Italian Senate.  In New York City on December 24, 1875,  [[John Celivergos Zachos]] invented a stenotype and filed patent number 175892 for type writers and phenotypic notation application.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=0hEzAQAAIAAJ&dq=Patent+No.+175%2C892&pg=PA1942 "The Commissioners of Patents' Journal"] ''US Patent 175892'' (August 4 1876): p. 1942</ref>  In 1879, [[Miles M. Bartholomew]] invented the shorthand machine. A French version was created by [[Marc Grandjean]] in 1909.  The direct ancestor of today's stenotype was created by [[Ward Stone Ireland]] in about 1913,<ref>{{Cite patent|country=US|number=1098115A|title=STENOGRAPHIC TYPE-WRITING MACHINE.|status=patent|pubdate=|gdate=1914-05-26|invent1=IRELAND|inventor1-first=WARD S.}}</ref> and the word "stenotype" was applied to his machine and its descendants sometime thereafter.

==Modern hardware==
[[File:Landtagsprojekt Sachsen-Anhalt by-RaBoe 2012 043.jpg|thumb|Stentura 8000LX steno writer]]
[[File:SOFT-HRUF.jpg|thumb|Open source stenotype hardware created by the SOFT/HRUF project]]
Most modern stenotype keyboards have more in common with computers than they do with typewriters or [[QWERTY]] computer keyboards. Most contain microprocessors, and many allow sensitivity adjustments for each individual key. They translate stenotype to the target language internally using user-specific dictionaries, and most have small display screens. They typically store a full day's work in non-volatile memory of some type, such as an [[SD card]]. These factors influence the price, along with [[economies of scale]], as only a few thousand stenotype keyboards are sold each year. {{As of|October 2013}}, student models, such as a Wave writer, sold for about US$1,500 and top-end models sold for approximately US$5,000. Machines that were 10 to 15 years old still resold for upward of $350.

The Open Steno Project<ref>[http://hardware.slashdot.org/story/14/08/12/1812250/type-225-words-per-minute-with-a-stenographic-keyboard-video Type 225 Words per Minute with a Stenographic Keyboard (Video)], Slashdot, Posted by Roblimo, August 12, 2014</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://openstenoproject.org/|title=The Open Steno Project|work=openstenoproject.org}}</ref> has written free open-source software, including [[Plover (software)|Plover]], and has developed cheap [[open-source hardware]] for stenography. Plover software translates keypresses to Stenotype on any modern keyboard, with a preference given to [[ortholinear]] keyboards that have [[NKRO]] functionality.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/openstenoproject/plover/wiki/Beginner's-Guide:-Get-Started-with-Plover#use-a-standard-qwerty-keyboard|title=Beginner's Guide: Get Started with Plover |website=[[GitHub]] | access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref>

=== Manufacturers ===
Stenograph is by far the largest manufacturer of American stenotype keyboards with an estimated market share in excess of 90%. Their top models are the NextGen and the Luminex CSE (Captioner Student Edition). There were two other large manufacturers in the 1980s (Xscribe, with the StenoRAM line and BaronData with the Transcriptor line).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1990/03/06/stenograph-closes-deal-for-barondata/ |title=Stenograph Closes Deal For Barondata |work=Chicago Tribune |date= March 6, 1990 |access-date=May 11, 2014}}</ref> Stenograph purchased both companies and discontinued their products. The current manufacturers in the US include:
* Advantage Software<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.eclipsecat.com/product/writers/passport-writer/passport-touch | title= Advantage Software, Eclipsecat.com | access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref> (Passport and Passport Touch)
* Neutrino Group<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.stenoworks.com/brands/The-Neutrino-Group%2CLLC.html|title=Infinity Writers, Neutrino Group, StenoWorks.com| access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref> (Gemini, Revolution, & Infinity writers)
* ProCAT<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.procat.com/ | title=ProCAT.com | access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref> (Stenopaq, Flash, Stylus, Impression, and Xpression)
* Stenograph<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.stenograph.com |title=Stenograph.com | access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref> (Stentura, élan Mira, Fusion, élan Cybra, Wave, Diamante, Luminex, and NexGen)
* Stenovations (LightSpeed)<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.stenovations.com/ |title=Stenovations.com | access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref> 
* Word Technologies (Tréal)<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.wordtechnologies.com/home.asp |title=WordTechnologies.com | access-date=Aug 1, 2019}}</ref>

=== Hobbyist keyboards ===
Many steno enthusiasts are making and selling keyboards designed for use with Plover,<ref name=":0" /> the open source steno software. Most of these keyboards range from about $100 to $200 and allow the user to use stenography on their computer through Plover. Vendors include:

* g Heavy Industries<ref>{{Cite web |last=Industries |first=g Heavy |title=g Heavy Industries |url=https://www.gboards.ca/ |access-date=2022-04-21 |website=g Heavy Industries}}</ref> (Georgi)
* Nolltronics<ref>{{Cite web |title=nolltronics – Making Steno Affordable |url=https://nolltronics.com/ |access-date=2022-04-21 |language=en-US}}</ref> (EcoSteno)
* SOFT/HRUF<ref>{{Cite web |title=SOFT/HRUF |url=https://softhruf.love/ |access-date=2022-04-21 |website=SOFT/HRUF}}</ref> (Splitography)
* StenoKeyboards<ref>{{Cite web |title=StenoKeyboards |url=https://stenokeyboards.com/ |access-date=2022-04-21 |website=StenoKeyboards |language=en}}</ref> (The Uni)
* Stenomod<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stenomod |url=https://stenomod.blogspot.com/ |access-date=2022-04-21 |website=stenomod.blogspot.com |language=en}}</ref> (TinyMod)
* Stenography Store<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stenography Store |url=https://stenography.store |access-date=2023-05-16 |website=Stenography Store |language=en}}</ref> (Starboard)

== Keyboard layout ==
[[File:Stenotype en layout.svg|thumb|right|A stenotype machine keyboard layout.]]

Stenotype keys normally are made of a hard, high-luster acrylic material with no markings. The accompanying image shows the [[chorded keyboard|keyboard]] layout of the American stenotype machine.

In "home position", the fingers of the left hand rest along the gap between the two main rows of keys to the left of the asterisk (little finger on the "<kbd>S</kbd>" to forefinger on the "<kbd>H</kbd>" and "<kbd>R</kbd>"). These fingers are used to generate initial consonants. The fingers of the right hand lie in the corresponding position to the right of the asterisk (forefinger on "<kbd>FR</kbd>" to little finger on "<kbd>TS</kbd>"), and are used for final consonants. The thumbs produce the vowels.

The system is roughly phonetic; for example the word ''cat'' would be written by a single stroke expressing the initial <kbd>K</kbd>, the vowel <kbd>A</kbd>, and the final <kbd>T</kbd>.

To enter a number, a user presses the number bar at the top of the keyboard at the same time as the other keys, much like the Shift key on a QWERTY-based keyboard. The illustration shows which lettered keys correspond to which digits. Numbers can be chorded, just as letters can. They read from left to right across the keyboard. It is possible to write 137 in one stroke by pressing the number bar along with <kbd>SP P</kbd>, but it takes three separate strokes to write 731. Many court reporters and stenocaptioners write out numbers phonetically instead of using the number bar.

There are various rule sets, known as ''theories'', to combine letters to make different sounds; different court reporters use different theories in their work.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2022-01-24|title=Theories and dictionaries|url=https://www.artofchording.com/introduction/theories-and-dictionaries.html|access-date=2022-02-22|website=Art of Chording}}</ref> Historically, reporters often created "briefs" (abbreviations) on-the-fly, and sometimes mixed theories, which could make it difficult for one reporter to read another reporter's notes, but current versions of theories are primarily designed for computerized translation using a standardized dictionary provided by the company that promulgates the theory, which forces reporters to stick with one theory and use only the specific combinations in that company's dictionary.  However, it is not uncommon for students and reporters to add a significant number of entries to a stock dictionary, usually when creating briefs of their own.

Some court reporters use ''[[scopist]]s'' to translate and edit their work. A scopist is a person who is trained in the phonetic writing system, English punctuation, and usually in legal formatting.  They are especially helpful when court reporters are working so much that they do not have time to edit their own work.  Both scopists and proofreaders work closely with court reporters to ensure an accurate transcript. The widespread use of realtime translation of the strokes has increased the demand for scopists to work simultaneously with the court reporter.  With transcripts produced on computer-aided transcription (CAT) software, a scopist no longer needs to have any knowledge of shorthand theories, because the software converts shorthand to text in real time via a dictionary.  However, it may still be helpful in some situations while scoping, as misstroked words may not translate and would appear in steno. Depending on availability of scopists and proofreaders, court reporters may use a scopist only to clean up a rough draft of their transcript, then proofread and certify the transcript themselves, or they may use neither and produce a final transcript by themselves, though this is a very time-consuming practice.

=== Steno paper ===
Steno paper has become almost obsolete with the advancement in paperless stenotype machines. When it is used, steno paper comes out of a stenotype machine at the rate of one row per chord, with the pressed letters printed out in 22 columns corresponding to the 22 keys, in the following order:

: <kbd>STKPWHRAO*EUFRPBLGTSDZ</kbd>

=== Chords ===
This is a basic chart of the letters of this machine. There are, however, different writing theories that represent some letters or sounds differently (e.g., the <kbd>*F</kbd> for final ''v'' in the chart below), and each court reporter develops personalized "briefs" and codes.

== Example ==
The following example shows how steno paper coming out of the machine represents an English sentence. Notice that key combinations can have different meanings depending on context. In the first stroke of the word ''example'', the <kbd>PL</kbd> combination refers to ''m''. In the second stroke of the word, that same key combination refers to the two letters ''pl''.
[[File:PrimerStenoMashinki.svg|upright=1.8|center|English text rendered in steno shorthand|frameless]]
Many words have been abbreviated: ''this'', ''of'' and ''from'' are chorded as ''th'', ''f'' and ''fr'', and ''machine'' and ''shorthand'' become ''mn'' and ''shand'' respectively.

== Canada ==
There is one NCRA-approved school in all of Canada that teaches stenotype: the captioning and court reporting program at NAIT (Northern Alberta Institute of Technology).<ref>{{Cite web|title=NCRA-Approved Court Reporting Programs {{!}} NCRA|url=https://www.ncra.org/home/students-teachers/Schools-and-programs/ncra-approved-court-reporting-programs|access-date=2021-07-14|website=www.ncra.org}}</ref> This program uses the <kbd>STKPWHRAO*EUFRPBLGTSDZ</kbd> keyboard layout. Graduates are trained to be [[Court reporter|court reporters]], [[Closed captioning|broadcast captioners]], or [[Communication access real-time translation|CART]] providers<ref>{{Cite web|title=Captioning & Court Reporting Career Opportunities|url=https://www.nait.ca/programs/captioning-court-reporting?term=2021-fall&overviewtabs=career-opportunities|website=NAIT}}</ref> and report a median income of $70,000 CAD between 2017 and 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|title=NAIT Graduate Median Salaries by Program Summary Cluster|url=https://www.nait.ca/mediansalaries|website=NAIT}}</ref> NAIT paused the program in September 2025, citing low enrollment. Some students from the 2024 cohort are reporting they cannot find work in their field, and students partway through the program are asking for tuition refunds.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zhao |first=Emma |date=Sep 22, 2026 |title=Former students say they're paying the price after NAIT axed its court reporting diploma |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/edmonton/nait-students-court-reporting-course |website=CBC News}}</ref>

== Other systems ==
=== English ===
In addition to the above American Stenotype layout of <kbd>STKPWHRAO*EUFRPBLGTSDZ</kbd> used internationally (Ward Stone Ireland 1913), there is also a Possum Palantype system still being used in the UK.<ref name="open-sys">{{cite web |title= Steno Layouts & Supported Languages |url= https://github.com/openstenoproject/plover/wiki/Steno-Layouts-&-Supported-Languages |website=GitHub |publisher=Open Steno Project |language=en}}</ref>

=== Italian ===
Two Stenotype layouts are in use for the [[Italian language]]: Michela and Melani. The former is in use by the Italian senate.<ref name="open-sys"/>

=== Korean ===
[[File:속기 스마트카스.png|thumb|A Korean stenotype of the CAS layout.]]
The main stenotype systems in Korea are CAS and Sorizava.<ref name="open-sys"/>

=== Other languages ===
* The Portuguese language has two stenotype systems. The Brazilian system uses the same layout as the American English one.<ref name="open-sys"/>
* The Japanese language uses a StenoWord system with ten remapped keys or a more conventional Sokutaipu system.<ref>{{cite web |title=Japanese on Plover · Issue #625 · openstenoproject/plover |url=https://github.com/openstenoproject/plover/issues/625 |website=GitHub |language=en}}</ref>
* As with the Korean language, Chinese stenotype layouts depend on the manufacturer, four of which are most commonly encountered in the market. A combination of chording and abbreviation is used.<ref>{{cite web |author1=清澈籁 |title=速录机的原理是什么？ |url=https://www.zhihu.com/question/21941424/answer/21106017 |website=Zhihu}}</ref>
